title: Read the constraints
prompt: A problem says `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`. Which complexity is the SLOWEST that will comfortably pass?
options: O(n log n) — about 1.7 million steps
explanation: Rule of thumb: ~10⁸ simple operations per second. n² at n=10⁵ is 10¹⁰ — far too slow. The constraint is a hint: find the O(n) or O(n log n) approach.

title: Classify the loop
prompt:
What's the time complexity?
`for (int i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) { ... }`
options: O(log n) — i halves every iteration
O(n/2), which is different from O(n)
explanation: Halving until 0 takes log₂(n) steps — the signature of binary search. And O(n/2) IS O(n): constants drop.

title: Space of recursion
prompt: A DFS recurses down a balanced binary tree of n nodes. Its space complexity is…
options: O(log n) — the call stack holds one path, and a balanced tree is log n deep
explanation: Only the current root-to-node path lives on the stack at once. Worst case (a degenerate, linked-list-shaped tree) is O(n) — worth mentioning in interviews.

title: The time-space trade
prompt: Your solution has nested loops: for each element, an inner loop searches for its complement. The standard optimization is…
options: Replace the inner search with a HashMap lookup: O(n²) time becomes O(n) time + O(n) space
explanation: "What lookup makes the inner loop O(1)?" is the most valuable question in array problems — it's exactly the Two Sum insight.

title: Count pairs in O(n)
prompt:
Return how many index pairs `i < j` satisfy `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`.

The obvious solution checks every pair with two nested loops — O(n²). Write the **O(n)** version: scan once, and for each `x` ask a HashMap "how many earlier values equal `target - x`?"

solution.explanation: When we reach `x`, every earlier value equal to `target - x` forms a valid pair with it, and the map already holds exactly how many of those there are. Looking up BEFORE recording `x` guarantees `i < j` and stops `x` from pairing with itself. One pass of O(1) map operations: O(n) time, O(n) space.

hints: For the current value `x`, which partner value would make a pair? How could you know instantly how many of those came before?
Keep a `Map<Integer, Integer>` counting the values seen so far. Add `seen.getOrDefault(target - x, 0)` to the answer.
Order matters: look up the partner first, then record `x` in the map, so an element never pairs with itself.
